tools.name: exec

format.definition:
start: pragma_source | plain_source
pragma_source: PRAGMA_LINE NEWLINE SOURCE
plain_source: SOURCE

PRAGMA_LINE: /[ \t]*\/\/ @exec:[^\r\n]*/
NEWLINE: /\r?\n/
SOURCE: /[\s\S]+/

tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.name: request_user_input
tools.description: Request user input for one to three short questions and wait for the response. This tool is only available in Plan mode.

questions.description: Questions to show the user. Prefer 1 and do not exceed 3

header.description: Short header label shown in the UI (12 or fewer chars).

options.description: Provide 2-3 mutually exclusive choices. Put the recommended option first and suffix its label with "(Recommended)". Do not include an "Other" option in this list; the client will add a free-form "Other" option automatically.

description.description: One short sentence explaining impact/tradeoff if selected.

question.description: Single-sentence prompt shown to the user.

tools.name: clock
tools.description: Tools for reading and waiting on time.

tools.name: sleep
tools.description: Pause execution for a specified duration. The sleep ends early when new input arrives for the active turn. Returns the elapsed wall-clock time.

duration_ms.description: How long to sleep in milliseconds. Must be between 1 and 43200000.

tools.name: collaboration
tools.description: Tools for spawning and managing sub-agents.

tools.name: followup_task
tools.description: Send a follow-up task to an existing non-root target agent and trigger a turn if it is idle. If the target is already running, deliver the task promptly at message boundaries while sampling, or after the pending tool call completes.

message.description: Message text to send to the target agent.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to send a follow-up task to (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Interrupt an agent's current turn, if any, and return its previous status. The agent remains available for messages and follow-up tasks.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to interrupt (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List live agents in the current root thread tree. Optionally filter by task-path prefix.

path_prefix.description: Task-path prefix filter without a trailing slash. Omit to list all live agents.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to an existing agent. The message will be delivered promptly. Does not trigger a new turn.

message.description: Message text to queue on the target agent.

target.description: Relative or canonical task name to message (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: spawn_agent
tools.description:
Available model overrides (optional; inherited parent model is preferred):
- `gpt-6.2-sol`: Fast, go-to model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6.2-astra`: Our most capable model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6.1-terra`: Efficient model that excels at visual understanding and computer use. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-sol`: Previous generation model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6-astra`: Previous generation model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6-sol`: Legacy model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-luna`: Fast and affordable model for easier tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-sol`: Legacy model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-terra`: Legacy balanced model for agentic coding. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-luna`: Legacy fast model for simpler tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.5`: Legacy coding model. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh. Service tiers: priority.
        Spawns an agent to work on the specified task. If your current task is `/root/task1` and you spawn_agent with task_name "task_3" the agent will have canonical task name `/root/task1/task_3`.
You are then able to refer to this agent as `task_3` or `/root/task1/task_3` interchangeably. However an agent `/root/task2/task_3` would only be able to communicate with this agent via its canonical name `/root/task1/task_3`.
The spawned agent will have the same tools as you and the ability to spawn its own subagents.

It will be able to send you and other running agents messages, and its final answer will be provided to you when it finishes.
The new agent's canonical task name will be provided to it along with the message.

Note that passing `fork_turns="none"` will not pass any surrounding context to the spawned subagent, which may cause the agent to lack the context it needs to complete its task, whereas `fork_turns="all"` will provide the subagent with all surrounding context.

fork_turns.description: Parent history to inherit. Defaults to `all`; use `none` to start without parent history. Only `all` and `none` are supported.

message.description: Initial plain-text task for the new agent.

model.description: Model override for the new agent. Omit unless an explicit override is needed.

reasoning_effort.description: Reasoning effort override for the new agent. Omit to inherit the parent effort.

task_name.description: Task name for the new agent. Use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

tools.name: wait_agent
tools.description: Wait for a mailbox update from any live agent, including queued messages and final-status notifications. The wait also ends early when new user input is steered into the active turn. Does not return the content; returns either a summary of which agents have updates (if any), an interruption summary for steered input, or a timeout summary if no activity arrives before the deadline.

timeout_ms.description: Timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000, min 10000, max 3600000.

tools.name: mcp__cua_repl
tools.description: UI automation through cua_repl using the initialized cua API.

tools.name: js
tools.description:
Control native apps or browsers on the user’s computer by reading or operating UI. Prefer purpose-built skills, connectors, APIs, or CLIs when available.

On the first invocation of `cua_repl`, or after resetting it, execute exactly one of the API calls shown below, optionally assigning its result to a variable. Do not add other API calls, waits, or snapshots to that invocation.
The tool result will include documentation and, when creating or selecting a tab or selecting an app, its initial UI state. Selecting a browser does not open a tab. Read that result before continuing.
Use only APIs described in the tool instructions or returned documentation.

When you need an inventory of available apps, browsers, and tabs, get a snapshot of all enabled surfaces. Otherwise, use the relevant entry point below:

```javascript
await cua.getState();
```

Use the first matching browser control option from the user's request:

For a tab @-mention (`mention=tab-v1`):
Pass the complete `plugin://...` URL to get the referenced tab.

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab({ mention: tabMentionUrl });
```

For an existing tab identified by URL in browser context (including the current IAB tab):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab({ url }, { browser: browserId });
```

Known tab ID (`tabId` or `providerTabId`) and browser (name or browser @-mention):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab(tabId, { browser: browserId });
```

To open a URL in the in-app browser (`@Browser`):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.createBrowserTab("iab", url, { visible: boolean });
```

To open a URL in another named browser: pass its name directly; do not call `getBrowser` first.

```javascript
let tab = await cua.createBrowserTab(browserName, url, browserOptions);
```

Known URL, only when the user has not specified a browser by name or @-mention:

```javascript
let browser = await cua.getBrowser({ url });
```

Browser IDs and options:

- `"mcpapps"`: use `cua.getBrowser({ id: "mcpapps" })` for existing full-screen MCP Apps in the task’s side panel.
- `"iab"` (in-app browser): in `createBrowserTab`, use `visible: true` to show the browser; `false` to keep it hidden.
- `"dot"` (Dot): use only when present in browser inventory. It accesses tabs on Dot's active main thread. `cua.getTab(tabId, { browser: "dot" })` selects an existing tab. `cua.createBrowserTab("dot", url, { visible: boolean })` creates one with the same visibility options as `"iab"`.
- `"chrome"` (@Chrome), `"edge"` (@Edge): pass a short, emoji-prefixed `sessionName` (e.g. `"🔎 Task"`) to `createBrowserTab` when starting a task.

If the user specifies an app to use, get the app by name, bundle ID, or path:

```javascript
let app = await cua.getApp("Example App");
```

To add other content to the tool result, use `nodeRepl.write(value)` for text or other values and `await nodeRepl.emitImage(image)` for images. The APIs listed above already display their documentation or UI state; do not wrap their results in `write` or `emitImage`.

If your context begins with a summary of an existing computer use task, call `await cua.rewriteDocumentation()` before continuing the computer use task to ensure you have a complete view of the necessary documentation.

Each `cua_repl.js` call opens or continues a browser activity. Keep consecutive calls together. The activity stays open across messages until you emit completion commentary.

**Manual takeover takes priority over the table below.** For a required manual browser step, call the documented takeover API before asking the user to act, unless takeover is already pending. Explain the required step in your final reply. Tab marking alone does not transfer control. While waiting for the user to finish and return control, emit no completion and make no CUA calls, even when answering side questions. The takeover API returning does not end this wait. When the user returns or unblocks you, resume browser work and apply the table. If they cancel, replace, or no longer need the browser work, close the activity before answering, even without another CUA call.

Completion is a standalone assistant commentary message containing only `::browser-complete{title="<headline>"}`. Never put it in a tool call or final reply. Use 3–6 words starting with a past-tense verb to describe the observed outcome. Omit identifiers.

After a user cancels pending browser work: commentary `::browser-complete{title="Stopped browser work"}`, then the final acknowledgement. No browser call is needed.

For an open browser activity:

| Next action                                   | Required output order                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Another CUA call                              | Continue without completion.                                                              |
| A non-CUA tool, final reply, or chat question | Finish required tab marking, emit completion, then take that action in the same response. |

With no open activity, emit no completion. Later CUA use requires a fresh completion at the next table boundary.

If you need a one-time sign-in code, information, or confirmation from the user, follow the table and ask in chat. One-time code entry alone does not require takeover. This tool is part of plugin `unified-computer-use`.

code.description: JavaScript to execute using the initialized cua_repl runtime.

timeout_ms.description: Optional execution timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000 (30 seconds) when omitted.

title.description: Short user-facing description of what this code block is doing. Prefer a few words in present-progressive form, such as 'Checking the mobile layout' or 'Comparing prices', over imperative or past-tense titles.

tools.name: js_reset
tools.description: Reset the persistent cua_repl JavaScript session. All JavaScript bindings are discarded. The next cua_repl.js call initializes a fresh runtime for the enabled surfaces. This does not close browser tabs or native apps, or erase their state. This tool is part of plugin `unified-computer-use`.

## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/Users/alexcallow/.agents/skills`
- `r1` = `/Users/alexcallow/.codex/skills/.system`
- `r2` = `/Users/alexcallow/.codex/plugins/cache/egm/egm/0.1.1/skills`
- `r3` = `/Users/alexcallow/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-bundled`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r1/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: API first-timers, Codex/Work Q&A. If the user already has an OpenAI API integration, skip this skill for API questions and use the developer docs. Read this skill before answering how Codex or ChatGPT Work behaves, where to find a feature, or how to configure or troubleshoot this app or coding agent. This includes conversation history, model and cache behavior, instruction precedence, permissions, and tool availability. Skip action requests, such as scheduling an automation, and tasks fully answered by supplied text or data. (file: r1/openai-docs/SKILL.md)

(file: r0/apollo-client/SKILL.md)
- built-in-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Codex desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Codex's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It is not for Codex in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (file: r0/synced/31fc0c17-6ddd-4792-886e-5cbd4fcd4b6f_1f3233f3-c0e3-424e-a407-80f78eb29aa1/built-in-browser/SKILL.md)
- chrome-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses Codex in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. description: Technical Copy Editor persona focused on clarity, precision, brevity, objective framing, and stripping fluff.

# Core Mandates (Universal Goldfish Context)

You are a specialized Goldfish subagent operating within the Elephant-Goldfish Model. You have been delegated a specific task by the root agent (the Elephant).

1. **Strict Read-Only Protocol**: You are a strictly read-only agent. You have NO tools to modify the workspace, write files, or compile code. Do not attempt to fix or refactor any code.
2. **Stateless Mindset (Goldfish Isolation)**: You evaluate plans with zero conversational history or external assumptions. You must read the document as a naive team member or fresh reader who has just joined the project.
3. **No Chitchat**: Avoid conversational filler. Focus exclusively on technical rationale and findings. Do not narrate your tool usage.

---

# Role

You are **Style Goldfish**.
You are a meticulous, objective Technical Copy Editor. You value clarity, precision, and brevity. You believe technical writing should be dry, direct, and factual. Your goal is to strip away fluff, jargon, and subjective opinions, ensuring the text reads as a professional engineering document.

---

# Instructions

Inspect the `Mode` parameter specified by the caller:

### IF Mode: BRAINSTORM (Upstream Concept Ideation)
Evaluate the raw feature concept for objective framing, clarity of terminology, and scope precision:
1. **Objective Framing**: Strip away hyperbole or vague buzzwords in the raw concept. Ensure problem statement and target goals are stated in clear, measurable terms.
2. **Scope Boundaries**: Flag ambiguous scope definitions that could lead to scope creep.
3. Report editorial findings and scope refinement requirements back to the orchestrator.

### IF Mode: REVIEW (Document Audit)
Audit the target document file and line range specified by the caller:

1. **Analyze Tone and Conciseness**: Parse the active target scope to evaluate the tone, word choice, and sentence structure.
2. **Verify Objectivity & Claim Calibration**: Ensure all claims are factual, measurable, and verifiable. Flag subjective evaluations of code quality or system performance, require every caveat to name a concrete reader/operator decision, and require every claim about existing or tested behavior to match its evidence.
3. **Evaluate for Fluff and Redundancy**: Identify and flag any filler words, buzzwords, or redundant phrasing that can be removed or simplified without losing meaning.
4. **Audit against the Standard (if provided)**: If a style standard is supplied, verify compliance with its specific style guidelines (e.g., active voice requirements, terminology constraints).

### Audit Vectors:
* **Hyperbole & Marketing Fluff**: Exaggerated or unprovable claims (e.g., "flawless execution," "revolutionary design," "fully eliminates all bugs").
* **Jargon & Buzzwords**: Non-precise terms that obscure meaning (e.g., "leverage the framework," "synergistic integration").
* **Filler Words & Wordiness**: Phrases that add noise instead of signal (e.g., "essentially," "simply run the command," "it is important to note that").
* **Subjective Quality Judgments**: Opinionated praise or critique of code, design, or legacy systems (e.g., "beautifully structured class," "terrible legacy parser").
* **Synonym Redundancy**: Adjacent or nearby words that repeat the same concept (e.g., "quick and rapid," "clean and elegant").
* **Defensive Caveats & Uncalibrated Claims (`DROP | CALIBRATE | RELOCATE | KEEP`)**: Blanket disclaimers for inactive failure modes, speculative hedging with no reachable operator decision, or capability claims about existing or tested behavior that outrun actual verification evidence. Classify each flagged sentence as `DROP` (no concrete reader decision), `CALIBRATE` (narrow claim to verified scope/evidence), `RELOCATE` (move operational caveat to the exact step where a user makes a choice), or `KEEP` (backed by concrete evidence; do not report it as a finding).

---

# Output Format

Report your findings back to the orchestrator in plain, natural language.

#### IF Mode: REVIEW
For each finding, include:
1. **Severity**: [Blocker | Major | Nit]
2. **Affected Scope**: Section heading or line numbers.
3. **Style Rationale**: Clear reasoning on why the phrasing is redundant, subjective, uncalibrated, or bloated. For a Defensive Caveats finding, add the recommended editorial action (`DROP`, `CALIBRATE`, or `RELOCATE`).

#### IF Mode: BRAINSTORM
For each framing or scope ambiguity, include:
1. **Severity**: [Blocker | Major | Nit]
2. **Dimension**: Objective Framing & Scope Precision
3. **Ambiguity Description**: Subjective claim, vague buzzword, or unmeasurable goal.
4. **Refinement Requirement**: Mandatory precision requirement for the Concepts Brief/PRD.

# Implementation Readiness Standard

This standard defines the quality bar for implementation plans and task lists.

## Core Principle

A plan passes if a competent engineer (or fresh AI session) who is unfamiliar
with the codebase can execute the plan and produce the correct changes on the
first attempt, without guessing, asking clarifying questions, or making
independent design choices.

## The Zero-Decision Rule

The plan must leave **zero design or architectural choices to the implementer**.
If the implementer must make design choices (including, but not limited to,
choosing a database schema, designing an API path, selecting a dependency, or
deciding how to handle a new edge case), the plan **fails** this standard. All
such decisions must be pre-determined and documented in the plan.

## Phasing & Checkpoints

The plan must partition the work into logical, incremental phases. Each phase
must leave the codebase in a stable, buildable, and testable state.

## Requirements (Non-Exhaustive Examples)

The plan must detail these areas if applicable to the proposed changes:

*   **Target Scope & File Boundary**: Explicit list of exact repository-relative
    file paths to be created, modified, or deleted, suitable for enforcing a
    Phase 5 write allowlist without unapproved adjacent refactors or
    opportunistic dependency additions. Use a directory glob only for generated
    output whose filenames can't be known in advance.
*   **Actionable Steps**: Precise logic changes, data transformations, and API
    updates for each file.
*   **Test Plan**: Specific test cases (happy path and edge cases) that must be
    implemented.
21:1.  **Shared Rules & Plugin-Root Paths**: Read the *Plugin-Root Resource Paths*, *Subagent Delegation (Goldfish Isolation)*, and *Shared Design & Review Constraints* sections of [execution instructions](../../resources/execution_instructions.md) (Claude Code: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/resources/execution_instructions.md`; pathless `<SKILL>`: `~/.gemini/config/plugins/egm/resources/execution_instructions.md`). Do not apply the drafting-only section here. Never call a bundled file missing after a failed skill-relative lookup, and pass spawned reviewers the resolved absolute paths of their persona file (`agents/<file>.md`) and document standard (`resources/document_standards/<name>.md`). If file tools cannot read `execution_instructions.md`, apply the inline rules below. Use direct dispatch instead of `egm-synthesizer` if nesting is unsupported (see [harnesses.md](../../docs/harnesses.md)); if no subagent tool exists, stop and tell the user that a review in the same context is not a Goldfish review.
22:2.  **Artifact-First & Style**: Never dump drafts or reports in chat; write every report to the working or artifact directory, share its path, and use direct plain English with adversarial scrutiny (never `"brilliant"`, `"great"`, `"smart"`, `"correct"`, `"perfect"`, `"excellent"`, `"spot-on"`, or apologies).
52:  2. `"Feature spec only (evaluate design without considering implementation)"` -> **Bypass Step 3** (`FeatureRange = 1..End`, `DetailedRange = N/A`), execute Stages 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> 8 with checkpoints, and halt cleanly after Stage 8 before Stage 9.
53:  3. `"Implementation plan only (evaluate design for implementation readiness)"` -> Run Step 3 to confirm `DetailedRange`, then jump directly to Stage 9.
71:| **5: Initial Zoom Out Review** | `full file` + `GoldfishContext` | Spawn `egm-synthesizer` (or direct) running `egm-zoom-out` (`agents/zoom_out.md`, standard `zoom-out-standard`) and `egm-inventive-catalyst` (`agents/inventive_catalyst.md`, `Mode: REVIEW`) in parallel | Write both to `zoom_out_report.md`; keep `"No false compromise detected"` when none found. |
72:| **6: Comprehension Test** | `FeatureRange` & `DetailedRange` (no `GoldfishContext`) | Spawn `egm-comprehension` (`agents/comprehension.md`) **directly** (never `egm-synthesizer`, which drops the paraphrase) with **no document standard** (tests self-containment; never `re-implementation-standard.md`, which asks for code detail forbidden in `FeatureRange`) | Write full output to `comprehension_report.md`: two verbatim paraphrase headings first, then findings (keep paraphrase even when there are no findings). |

1	# Frame Inventory — Exercise Instructions
     2	
     3	## 1. Scenario
     4	
     5	In the **out-of-home (OOH) media** industry, advertisers buy time on physical
     6	display surfaces such as roadside billboards, transport platforms, mall
     7	screens, and bus shelters. Each surface is referred to as a **frame**, and an
     8	operator's catalogue of frames — including their location, size, format,
     9	status, and commercial attributes — is collectively known as the **frame
    10	inventory**. Keeping that inventory accurate matters: every downstream process
    11	(planning, pricing, booking, reporting) depends on it.
    12	
    13	For this exercise the candidate will build a small but realistic service for
    14	managing OOH frame inventory. Scoping is part of the exercise: the candidate
    15	is not expected to deliver every feature one could imagine, but to pick a
    16	meaningful subset and deliver it well.
    17	
    18	## 2. What we provide
    19	
    20	This repository is the starting point. It is intentionally minimal so the
    21	candidate can make their own architectural choices, but it includes enough
    22	infrastructure to skip the boilerplate and start delivering business value
    23	straight away.
    24	
    25	| Path                  | Contents                                                                          |
    26	| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    27	| `src/backend/`        | Bare Spring Boot 3.5 + Java 21 module (Gradle). Exposes only `/api/health`.       |
    28	| `src/frontend/`       | Next.js + React 19 + TypeScript module that calls the backend `/api/health` on boot. |
    29	| `docker-compose.yml`  | One-command infra: backend, frontend, MongoDB, Postgres, OpenSearch + Dashboards.  |
    30	| `data/`               | Extract from the legacy system — `inventory_frame.csv` (~1.3k OOH frame rows).    |
    31	| `design-system/`      | Design system the frontend must be built against — components, tokens, guidance.  |
    32	| `README.md`           | How to run the stack locally, ports, and credentials for the bundled services.    |
    33	
    34	> **A note on the suggested infrastructure.** The `docker-compose.yml` file
    35	> is a starting point, not a requirement. The candidate is free to swap any
    36	> of these services for tooling they prefer (a different database, search
    37	> engine, message broker, hosting model, etc.) as long as the final stack
    38	> still runs end-to-end with a single command. If the candidate does choose
    39	> to use the services provided here, they should pick **one** of the two
    40	> datastores for their domain data — either `mongodb` *or* `postgres`,
    41	> not both — and remove the service they don't need (along with its volume)
    42	> so the stack reflects the design actually built.
    43	
    44	In addition, the candidate receives:
    45	
    46	- A **provisioned OpenAI Codex API key**. Use of an AI coding assistant is
    47	  explicitly expected — we want to see how the candidate collaborates with a
    48	  model, not whether they can hand-write every line.
    49	
    50	## 3. Features
    51	
    52	The candidate should deliver the following features:
    53	
    54	1. **Add a frame.** A user can create a new frame through the application and
    55	   see it persisted in the inventory.
    56	2. **Edit a frame.** A user can amend an existing frame's attributes and have
    57	   the changes saved.
    58	3. **Bulk upload frames from a CSV.** A user can upload a CSV through the
    59	   application and have the rows ingested into the inventory. The supplied
    60	   `data/inventory_frame.csv` is the file to validate this feature
    61	   against. This is a user-driven feature of the running app, not a one-off
    62	   bootstrap step.
    63	4. **View a frame's history.** A user can see the audit trail of changes to
    64	   any given frame.
    65	
    66	How these features are surfaced, structured, and tested is left to the
    67	candidate's judgement.
    68	
    69	## 4. Domain data
    70	
    71	The shape of a frame is anchored by the legacy export shipped at
    72	`data/inventory_frame.csv` (~1,300 rows) and by the prototype in
    73	`design-system/`. The candidate is expected to inspect both and design a
    74	domain model they are comfortable defending.
    75	
    76	At a high level, each frame in the export carries:
    77	
    78	- **Identity** — a frame identifier, plus references to downstream systems
    79	  (Broadsign, pricing, linked frames).
    80	- **Location** — country, region, town, postcode, latitude/longitude,
    81	  address, and distance to the nearest school.
    82	- **Site & position** — the kind of place the frame lives in (station,
    83	  underground, roadside, airport, etc.) and where on that site it sits.
    84	- **Format** — classic vs digital, format code, dimensions / pixels /
    85	  aspect ratio, illumination, number of slots, size grouping.
    86	- **Lifecycle** — created/modified timestamps, status, and a status reason.
    87	- **Commercials** — impact weight, pricing grade, production rate card,
    88	  premium flag.
    89	
    90	The legacy column names and groupings are not prescriptive — the candidate
    91	should design the domain model that best fits the features in §3, and
    92	document the assumptions they made along the way.
    93	
    94	## 5. Additional Requirements
    95	
    96	Install and use the **[Entire CLI](https://entire.io)**. Entire hooks into the
    97	candidate's git workflow and, on every push, captures the Codex agent
    98	sessions that produced the changes and links them to the corresponding
    99	commits as *checkpoints*. The result is a searchable record of how the
   100	solution was actually built: the prompts used, the iterations the candidate
   101	went through, the suggestions they accepted, and — just as important — the
   102	ones they rejected or refined.
   103	
   104	This is not about surveillance; it is about giving us a fair signal of
   105	**how** the candidate works with AI tooling. We are far less interested in
   106	whether code came from a human keystroke or a model completion than in
   107	whether the candidate exercised judgement, scoped well, and reviewed the
   108	output critically.
   109	
   110	> **Note:** Codex support in Entire is currently in preview. The candidate
   111	> should follow Entire's setup documentation for the latest supported
   112	> workflow.
   113	
   114	## 6. Submission
   115	
   116	When the candidate is ready, they should share a **public GitHub repository**
   117	containing their solution. The repository must include:
   118	
   119	- All source code and anything else required to run the solution.
   120	- A README explaining how to run it, the design decisions taken, and the
   121	  trade-offs made.
   122	- The Entire **checkpoints branch** with the captured Codex sessions linked
   123	  to commits, so we can review the AI collaboration alongside the code.
   124	
   125	There is no fixed deadline; we recommend timeboxing the exercise to a few
   126	focused sessions rather than open-ended work. If something blocks progress,
   127	note it in the README rather than over-investing time on it.

     1	# Frame inventory schema and version history
     2	
     3	- **Author** Alex Callow
     4	- **Date** 2026-11-26
     5	
     6	## Overview
     7	
     8	PostgreSQL stores a stable `frame_id` for each frame and a separate row for each accepted version. The [Flyway migration](../../src/backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_frame_inventory.sql) creates the empty inventory tables on Spring Boot startup.
     9	
    10	The supplied extract contains 1,000 rows, 1,000 distinct frame IDs, and 45 fields. The exercise calls for a user-driven import. [CSV](../../data/inventory_frame.csv) [Exercise requirements](../../INSTRUCTIONS.md#L52-L64)
    11	
    12	## CSV field mapping
    13	
    14	CSV values arrive as text. A blank optional value becomes SQL `NULL`. Counts and value sets describe the supplied extract.
    15	
    16	| CSV fields | Observed representation | PostgreSQL mapping |
    17	| --- | --- | --- |
    18	| `frame_id` | Ten decimal digits, unique and populated in all rows | `frame.frame_id text` primary key. The prototype also uses alphanumeric frame IDs. |
    19	| `created_date`, `modified_date` | Date and time to seconds, without offsets | `frame_version.source_created_at` and `source_modified_at`, both `timestamp without time zone`. |
    20	| `country_code`, `region`, `town` | Codes and names. One country, 12 regions, 172 towns | Country code and region name form the region's natural key. Town name is scoped to a region. Each table also has a generated primary key. |
    21	| `postcode` | UK postcode with a space, 484 distinct | `postcode` row keyed by generated ID, unique on `(town_id, postcode)`. |
    22	| `postcode_area`, `postcode_district`, `postcode_sector`, `postcode_unit` | Text fragments, some containing letters | Derive from the postcode. The four fragments reconstruct it exactly in all 1,000 rows. |
    23	| `longitude`, `latitude` | Signed decimal degrees | Exact `numeric` columns on `frame_version`, with valid coordinate ranges. |
    24	| `location` | `POINT (latitude longitude)` text | Derive from the scalar coordinates if an export requires the legacy format. All 1,000 rows contain the same pair in this order. |
    25	| `site_no`, `inventory_site_no`, `panel_number` | Identifiers. Site and panel numbers can contain leading zeros | Independent `text` fields on `frame_version`. |
    26	| `location_id` | Identifier, 13 blanks | Nullable `text` on `frame_version`. In 67 rows the populated value differs from the normalized postcode. |
    27	| `environment`, `address`, `station`, `airport` | Text. Station has 593 blanks and airport has 887 | `text` on `frame_version`, with the optional site names nullable. |
    28	| `type_classic_digital`, `format`, `size_group_code` | Codes. Nine distinct combinations | `frame_format` row keyed by generated ID, unique on the three codes. Codes stay as text, including size groups such as `006`. |
    29	| `size_code`, `aspect_ratio_code`, `t_size` | Codes and labels. `t_size` has 57 blanks | `text` columns on `frame_version`. |
    30	| `pixel_height`, `pixel_width` | Positive integers, 28 blanks in each column | Nullable `integer` dimensions on `frame_version`. |
    31	| `illumination_type_id`, `number_of_slots`, `distance_to_closest_school` | Integer code, count, and distance | `integer` on `frame_version`. The distance is assumed to be in metres, consistent with the prototype. |
    32	| `status`, `status_reason` | Text. Every row is `LIVE` and all reasons are blank | Status and nullable reason on `frame_version`. |
    33	| `impact_weight` | Decimal, six blanks | Nullable exact `numeric` on `frame_version`. |
    34	| `premium` | `0` or `1` | `boolean` on `frame_version`. |
    35	| `production_rate_card`, `production_rate_card_legacy` | Both columns are blank throughout | Separate nullable `text` fields until the source contract establishes how they relate. |
    36	| `pricing_grade` | Text, 869 blanks | Nullable `text` on `frame_version`. |
    37	| `price_entity_id`, `broadsign_display_unit_id`, `broadsign_frame_id`, `broadsign_domain_id` | Opaque codes. Broadsign fields have 3, 979, and 29 blanks respectively | `frame_version_external_reference` rows keyed by `(version_id, reference_type)`, with identifier values as text. Values can recur across frames. |
    38	| `linked_frame_ids` | Comma-separated IDs, present in four rows | Ordered `frame_version_link` rows keyed by `(version_id, position)`, with each target ID as text. Each supplied list includes its source frame and a peer. |
    39	
    40	## Relational structure
    41	
    42	- `frame_version` has a primary key and foreign keys to `frame`, `postcode`, and `frame_format`. `postcode` references `town`, which references `region`. When lookup values change, the writer creates or reuses a row with the new values so earlier versions keep their original values.
    43	- External references and linked frame IDs belong to the version that carried them. Both child tables reference that version. Resolve a linked target by joining its source ID to `frame.frame_id`. This lets a partial upload preserve a reference before its target arrives.
    44	- Keep address, position, and coordinates on the version. Eight `site_no` values map to multiple `inventory_site_no` values, and 95 `inventory_site_no` values map to multiple `site_no` values. Even matching pairs can have different coordinates and addresses.
    45	- Store format and size-group codes independently in the format tuple. Their values line up one-to-one in this extract. A wider export may contain combinations absent here. Status, technology, and slot count also vary in the intended product even though each is uniform in this sample.
    46	
    47	## Versioning contract
    48	
    49	| Incoming CSV row | Result |
    50	| --- | --- |
    51	| First row for a frame | Insert the stable frame and its first current version. |
    52	| Strictly older source `modified_date` | Leave the current row, links, and history as they were. |
    53	| Equal or newer source `modified_date` | Set the old row's `is_current` to false and its `valid_to` to the transition instant. Insert a current version with `valid_from` set to that same instant. |
    54	
    55	The migration uses `timestamptz` for half-open validity intervals `[valid_from, valid_to)`. Check constraints require a positive interval for closed versions and tie `is_current` to whether `valid_to` is null. A partial unique index enforces at most one current version per frame.
    56	
    57	The future CSV upload, create, and edit paths will share a Spring `@Transactional` service. The service creates or locks the stable frame row before comparing source timestamps. It closes the current version and appends its replacement in the same transaction. The transition time must be later than the previous version's start, including when two rows are accepted in one transaction.
    58	
    59	Source timestamps retain their original wall-clock values. Equal timestamps append a new version, including when the same file is uploaded again. Manual creation can start with null source timestamps. Manual edits carry forward the last accepted source timestamp. History starts with the first accepted version because the CSV contains one snapshot per frame.
    60	
    61	## Alternatives weighed
    62	
    63	- One wide mutable row has a simple current read and loses revisions. A second mutable current table would duplicate the version data and require another write on each transition. Index the current versions in the history table.
    64	- One table per category code would add joins and introduce catalog rules that the extract cannot establish. Share the repeated region, town, postcode, and format tuples and keep frame-specific values with each historical version.
    65	- A foreign key from each linked target to an existing frame gives immediate referential integrity and forces partial uploads to wait for every target. Preserve each source target identifier and enforce the owner foreign key. An unresolved target can join to its frame once that frame arrives.
    66	
    67	## Scope and verification
    68	
    69	Flyway V1 defines the tables, keys, validity checks, and indexes. CSV parsing, the shared write service, and the upload, edit, and history screens are future application work.
    70	
    71	Flyway applied V1 on PostgreSQL 18.6 and skipped it on restart. A rollback-only check loaded all 1,000 CSV rows and exercised the database constraints. The [backend README](../../src/backend/README.md) describes how to verify the migration using `flyway_schema_history`.

     2	
     3	package frameinventory.v1;
     4	
     5	option java_package = "com.global.ct.frameinventory.grpc.v1";
     6	option java_multiple_files = true;
     7	option java_outer_classname = "FramesProto";
     8	
     9	import "google/protobuf/empty.proto";
    10	import "google/protobuf/timestamp.proto";
    11	
    12	service FrameManagement {
    13	  rpc ListFrames(ListFramesRequest) returns (ListFramesResponse);
    14	  rpc GetFrame(GetFrameRequest) returns (Frame);
    15	  rpc GetFrameHistory(GetFrameHistoryRequest) returns (GetFrameHistoryResponse);
    16	  rpc CreateFrame(CreateFrameRequest) returns (Frame);
    17	  rpc UpdateFrame(UpdateFrameRequest) returns (Frame);
    18	  rpc DeleteFrame(DeleteFrameRequest) returns (google.protobuf.Empty);
    19	}
    20	
    21	message ListFramesRequest {
    22	  // Zero-based page. Defaults to 0.
    23	  optional int32 page = 1;
    24	  // Defaults to 25. Valid values are 1 through 50.
    25	  optional int32 size = 2;
    26	}
    27	
    28	message ListFramesResponse {
    29	  repeated Frame items = 1;
    30	  int32 page = 2;
    31	  int32 size = 3;
    32	  bool has_next = 4;
    33	}
    34	
    35	message GetFrameRequest {
    36	  string frame_id = 1;
    37	}
    38	
    39	message GetFrameHistoryRequest {
    40	  string frame_id = 1;
    41	}
    42	
    43	message GetFrameHistoryResponse {
    44	  // Newest first, with version ID descending as a tie break.
    45	  repeated Frame versions = 1;
    46	}
    47	
    48	message CreateFrameRequest {
    49	  // A case-sensitive identifier that can be used only once.
    50	  string frame_id = 1;
    51	  FrameData attributes = 2;
    52	}
    53	
    54	message UpdateFrameRequest {
    55	  string frame_id = 1;
    56	  // Must match the current version.
    57	  int64 expected_version_id = 2;
    58	  // Replaces writable attributes. Omitted optional fields are cleared.
    59	  FrameData attributes = 3;
    60	}
    61	
    62	message DeleteFrameRequest {
    63	  string frame_id = 1;
    64	  // If absent the delete applies to the current version.
    65	  optional int64 expected_version_id = 2;
    66	}
    67	
    68	message Frame {
    69	  string frame_id = 1;
    70	  int64 version_id = 2;
    71	  google.protobuf.Timestamp valid_from = 3;
    72	  google.protobuf.Timestamp valid_to = 4;
    73	  bool current = 5;
    74	  optional string change_source = 6;
    75	  optional string closed_by_change_source = 7;
    76	  // Local source timestamps in ISO 8601 format without an offset.
    77	  optional string source_created_at = 8;
    78	  optional string source_modified_at = 9;
    79	  FrameData attributes = 10;
    80	  map<string, string> external_references = 11;
    81	  repeated string linked_frame_ids = 12;
    82	}
    83	
    84	message FrameData {
    85	  // Manual writes accept LIVE, PENDING, MAINTENANCE, BLOCKED, or DRAFT.
    86	  string status = 1;
    87	  optional string status_reason = 2;
    88	  optional string site_no = 3;
    89	  optional string inventory_site_no = 4;
    90	  optional string panel_number = 5;
    91	  optional string location_id = 6;
    92	  optional string environment = 7;
    93	  optional string address = 8;
    94	  optional string station = 9;
    95	  optional string airport = 10;
    96	  // Decimal strings retain PostgreSQL numeric precision.
    97	  optional string latitude = 11;
    98	  optional string longitude = 12;
    99	  optional int32 distance_to_closest_school = 13;
   100	  FrameLocation location = 14;
   101	  FrameFormat format = 15;
   102	  optional string size_code = 16;
   103	  optional string aspect_ratio_code = 17;
   104	  optional string t_size = 18;
   105	  optional int32 pixel_height = 19;
   106	  optional int32 pixel_width = 20;
   107	  optional int32 illumination_type_id = 21;
   108	  optional int32 number_of_slots = 22;
   109	  optional string impact_weight = 23;
   110	  bool premium = 24;
   111	  optional string production_rate_card = 25;
   112	  optional string production_rate_card_legacy = 26;
   113	  optional string pricing_grade = 27;
   114	}
   115	
   116	message FrameLocation {

   120	  string postcode = 4;
   121	}

1	# Backend
     2	
     3	## Overview
     4	
     5	The backend is a Java 21 Spring Boot application. Spring gRPC serves frame management on port 9090. Spring MVC and Actuator serve health endpoints on port 8080. Spring Boot applies Flyway migrations against PostgreSQL at startup. The Docker image builds a Spring Boot JAR and runs it on Java 21. [build.gradle:languageVersion] [build.gradle:dependencies] [Dockerfile:RUN] [Dockerfile:ENTRYPOINT]
     6	
     7	## Subdirectories & Boundaries
     8	
     9	- [Source tree](./src/README.md) contains the application and its runtime configuration.
    10	- [Inventory migration](./src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_frame_inventory.sql) creates the frame, version history, and related tables.
    11	- [Frame inventory schema](../../docs/frame-inventory-schema/frame-inventory-schema.md) maps the CSV fields and describes the shared Spring write transaction.
    12	
    13	## Local development
    14	
    15	Start the Compose PostgreSQL service from the repository root with
    16	`docker compose up -d --wait postgres`. From `src/backend`, run
    17	`./gradlew bootRun` with Java 21. The local JDBC defaults connect to the
    18	Compose database. Set `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL`, `SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME`,
    19	and `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD` when connecting to a different database.
    20	
    21	## Verification
    22	
    23	From `src/backend`, run `./gradlew test` with Java 21 and Docker available. The
    24	suite covers unit tests and calls the gRPC service through a generated client
    25	against PostgreSQL 18.6 using Testcontainers. Flyway applies both schema
    26	migrations during the integration tests.
    27	
    28	## Frame management API
    29	
    30	The [Protobuf definition](src/main/proto/frameinventory/v1/frames.proto) declares
    31	the six RPCs. Run `./gradlew generateProto` to generate the Java messages and
    32	stubs. The [API contract](../../docs/frame-management-grpc-api.md#grpc-contract) describes
    33	pagination, request fields, errors, and version checks.
    34	
    35	With the backend running, call the service from `src/backend` using `grpcurl`.
    36	
    37	```sh
    38	grpcurl -plaintext -import-path src/main/proto -proto frameinventory/v1/frames.proto \
    39	  -d '{"page":0,"size":25}' localhost:9090 frameinventory.v1.FrameManagement/ListFrames
    40	```
    41	
    42	The backend writes structured JSON logs to the console. Set
    43	`LOGGING_LEVEL_COM_GLOBAL_CT_FRAMEINVENTORY_FRAME=DEBUG` to include frame RPC
    44	parameters, version checks, lookup results, and handled client errors.
    45	
    46	## Sentry error reporting
    47	
    48	Set `SENTRY_DSN` to the DSN of the backend's Sentry project and set
    49	`SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT` to the environment name, such as `staging`. The environment
    50	defaults to `local`. An empty or unset DSN disables error reporting.
    51	
    52	Export the variables before running `./gradlew bootRun` from `src/backend`.
    53	For Docker Compose, export the same variables or set them in an untracked
    54	`.env` file at the repository root, then run `docker compose up --build -d backend`
    55	to rebuild and apply the settings.
    56	
    57	To verify reporting, use a non-production Sentry project or environment. In a
    58	local checkout, temporarily make a controller handler throw an
    59	`IllegalStateException` with a unique test message and call that route. Confirm
    60	the event appears in Sentry with the expected stack trace and environment tag,
    61	then link the event on the issue. Remove the temporary exception and confirm
    62	`curl --fail http://localhost:8080/api/health` succeeds with the DSN configured
    63	and again after restarting the backend with the DSN unset.
     1	# Frame Inventory
     2	
     3	Monorepo scaffold for the frame-inventory take-home exercise.
     4	
     5	## System Overview
     6	
     7	The Next.js page calls the Spring Boot health endpoint through a same-origin rewrite. Docker Compose runs both modules alongside PostgreSQL, OpenSearch, OpenSearch Dashboards, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Alloy, and the OpenTelemetry Collector. The exercise provides a legacy export in `data/inventory_frame.csv` and describes the inventory features in `INSTRUCTIONS.md`.
     8	
     9	Bring the whole stack up with one command.
    10	
    11	```bash
    12	docker compose up --build
    13	```
    14	
    15	Once PostgreSQL is healthy, the backend applies pending Flyway migrations during startup.
    16	
    17	If you have `just` installed, run `just` to list the available recipes.
    18	
    19	| Command | Purpose |
    20	|---------|---------|
    21	| `just up` | Build and start the whole stack in the foreground. |
    22	| `just down` | Stop the stack and retain its named data volumes. |
    23	| `just compose logs -f backend` | Pass arguments through to Docker Compose. |
    24	| `just migrate` | Run Flyway on its own in a one-off backend container. |
    25	
    26	## Subdirectories & System Boundaries
    27	
    28	- [Application source](./src/README.md) contains the Spring Boot backend, Apollo Server BFF, and Next.js frontend.
    29	- [Design system](./design-system/README.md) contains the prototype, sample frame data, and visual conventions for the exercise.
    30	
    31	## Services
    32	
    33	`docker compose up` starts the following services.
    34	
    35	| Service               | Host port | Container port | Notes                                                  |
    36	|-----------------------|-----------|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
    37	| frontend              | 3000      | 3000           | Next.js dev server, proxies `/api` to the backend     |
    38	| bff                   | 4000      | 4000           | Apollo Sandbox and the frame inventory GraphQL API     |
    39	| backend               | 8080      | 8080           | Spring Boot, exposes `GET /api/health`                 |
    40	| postgres              | 5432      | 5432           | Spring Boot applies the inventory schema via Flyway    |
    41	| opensearch            | 9200, 9600 | 9200, 9600    | Single-node, security plugin disabled for local use    |
    42	| opensearch-dashboards | 5601      | 5601           | UI for the OpenSearch cluster above                    |
    43	| prometheus            | 9091      | 9090           | Scrapes Spring Boot and Apollo metrics every 15 seconds |
    44	| otel-collector        | 9464      | 9464           | Scrapes Spring Boot metrics for local inspection       |
    45	| grafana               | 3001      | 3000           | Queries provisioned Prometheus and Loki data            |
    46	
    47	### Credentials
    48	
    49	| Service               | User       | Password       | Database         |
    50	|-----------------------|------------|----------------|------------------|
    51	| postgres              | `app`      | `app`          | `frames`         |
    52	| opensearch            | n/a        | n/a            | n/a              |
    53	| grafana               | `admin`    | `admin`         | n/a              |
    54	
    55	## Global Invariants
    56	
    57	- The Next.js rewrite preserves the `/api/` path and uses `BACKEND_URL` as its destination origin. Compose sets it to `http://backend:8080`. `[src/frontend/next.config.ts:rewrites]` `[docker-compose.yml:services.frontend.environment.BACKEND_URL]`
    58	- The health page expects `status`, `service`, and `timestamp` from `GET /api/health`. The backend supplies those fields directly. `[src/frontend/src/app/page.tsx:HealthResponse]` `[src/backend/src/main/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/HealthController.java:health]`
    59	
    60	## Global Side Effects
    61	
    62	- Opening the frontend requests `/api/health`, which the Next.js server forwards to the backend. The response reports the current time from the backend clock. `[src/frontend/src/app/page.tsx:Home]` `[src/frontend/next.config.ts:rewrites]` `[src/backend/src/main/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/HealthController.java:health]`
    63	- Docker Compose publishes service ports and creates named volumes for PostgreSQL and OpenSearch. OpenSearch Dashboards connects to OpenSearch on the Compose network. `[docker-compose.yml:services]` `[docker-compose.yml:volumes]` `[docker-compose.yml:services.opensearch-dashboards.environment.OPENSEARCH_HOSTS]`
    64

    66	
    67	- From `src/backend`, run `./gradlew test`.

    69	
    70	### Git hooks
    71	
    72	Install [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/#installation), then run `pre-commit install`
    73	from the repository root to install both Git hooks. The `pre-commit` hook checks
    74	YAML, JSON, and merge conflict markers, and runs ESLint when staged changes touch
    75	`src/frontend/`. Install the frontend dependencies with `npm ci --prefix src/frontend`
    76	before committing frontend changes.
    77	
    78	The `commit-msg` hook uses Commitlint to enforce the Conventional Commits format
    79	documented in [AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md). Commitlint requires Node.js 22.12 or newer.
    80	
    81	Run `pre-commit run --all-files` to check the whole repository.
    82	
    83	### Smoke test
    84	
    85	Once the stack is up, check the service entry points.
    86	
    87	- Open <http://localhost:3000> — the page calls `/api/health` and prints the JSON response.
    88	- Hit the backend directly: <http://localhost:8080/api/health>.
    89	- Open [Apollo Sandbox](http://127.0.0.1:4000) and run the [frame list query](./src/bff/README.md).
    90	
    91	### Backend metrics
    92	
    93	- Open [Prometheus Targets](http://127.0.0.1:9091/targets) and wait for the
    94	  `frame-inventory-backend` target to show **UP**. It scrapes
    95	  `http://backend:8080/actuator/prometheus` on the Compose network.
    96	- Open [Grafana](http://127.0.0.1:3001), sign in with the initial credentials

    98	  default Prometheus data source. A value of `1` confirms the backend is being scraped.
    99	- Open [Frame Inventory Backend](http://127.0.0.1:3001/d/frame-inventory-backend/frame-inventory-backend)
   100	  for HTTP and gRPC request rate, errors, p50, p95, and p99 latency, and resource saturation.
   101	  Generate API traffic and allow at least two Prometheus scrapes for request graphs
   102	  to populate.
   103	- The **Frame inventory activity** section shows committed creates, updates, and
   104	  soft deletes, plus successful gRPC reads and version conflicts. The totals cover
   105	  the dashboard time range. Rejected or rolled-back writes and repeated deletes
   106	  that change no data are excluded from the totals.
   107	
   108	Prometheus and Grafana listen on localhost. Their named volumes keep metrics
   109	and Grafana settings across restarts.
   110	
   111	### BFF metrics
   112	
   113	Run `docker compose up -d --build bff prometheus grafana`. If Prometheus was
   114	already running, reload its scrape configuration with
   115	`docker compose restart prometheus`. Confirm that `frame-inventory-bff` is

   129	
   130	Run `docker compose up -d --build bff grafana`. Alloy reads the backend and

   142	- Backend — `{service_name="backend"}`

     1	# Bulk CSV inventory import
     2	
     3	Author: Alex Callow
     4	Date: 2026-11-26
     5	
     6	## Overview
     7	
     8	An inventory operator uploads inventory_frame.csv directly to S3 using a presigned URL. The BFF delegates job creation to Spring Boot, which records AWAITING_UPLOAD and assigns uploads/{jobId}/inventory_frame.csv. An S3-triggered Lambda sends the upload event to SQS. Spring Boot moves the job to PENDING and starts Temporal workflow csv-import-{jobId}. SQS retries failed delivery and a DLQ listener records dispatch failures.
     9	
    10	The worker streams the CSV into job-scoped UNLOGGED PostgreSQL staging in batches and heartbeats during loading. It records invalid rows in import_row_errors and applies set-based writes with MERGE RETURNING where appropriate. The proposed six-table target and frame history must be reconciled with the repository's existing versioned schema. Inventory changes and outbox records must commit together.
    11	
    12	## Agreed import behavior
    13	
    14	- A newer source timestamp creates a version. An equal timestamp and matching content hash is a no-op. An older timestamp produces STALE_RECORD. An equal timestamp with different content produces TIMESTAMP_COLLISION_CONFLICT and records both hashes. Skipped conflicts result in COMPLETED_WITH_ERRORS.
    15	- The explicit forceOverwrite flag accepts stale and same-timestamp conflicts. The new version preserves source_modified_date and records FORCED_OVERWRITE and import_job_id. Close and open at one database-generated boundary strictly later than the locked current valid_from.
    16	- DELTA is the default and leaves absent frames alone. FULL_SNAPSHOT requires an explicit GLOBAL scope or validated partition scope using country, region or environment. Every identifiable frame ID in the file counts as present, including rows with invalid payloads.
    17	- FULL_SNAPSHOT soft-retires absent active frames in scope with MISSING_FROM_FULL_SNAPSHOT. Abort if more than 10% of scoped active frames would retire. A malformed-row rate above 5% must prevent retirement. Whether to fail the whole snapshot is open.
    18	
    19	## Analysis
    20	
    21	All seven Goldfish lenses completed review. The recommendations below are proposed decisions for RFC alignment.
    22	
    23	### Delivery and recovery
    24	
    25	- Bind each job to one immutable object. Sign the exact key and the create-only PUT condition (If-None-Match: *), enable S3 versioning, and persist the accepted version ID so every retry reads the same bytes. Keep the object through the retry and reconciliation window. Validate the bucket, decoded key, object version, and size before dispatch. [S3 conditional writes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-writes.html) [S3 event delivery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/notification-how-to-event-types-and-destinations.html)
    26	- Record PENDING conditionally, invoke Temporal with the job-derived workflow ID, and acknowledge SQS only after start or after confirming the same job's workflow already exists. Configure both running-ID conflict and closed-ID reuse policies. A crash between the DB write and Temporal start leaves a retryable PENDING job. A lost start response must be reconciled before any DLQ transition to FAILED. Guard terminal states and fence a late starter with conditional job transitions before it can apply inventory. Reconcile old AWAITING_UPLOAD and PENDING jobs against S3 and Temporal, and cover Lambda delivery failures separately from consumer DLQ failures. [Temporal workflow ID policies](https://docs.temporal.io/develop/java/nexus/development-walkthrough/send-messages)
    27	- Stage by job ID, attempt generation, and logical CSV row number. Record observed frame IDs independently of row validity. Mark a generation complete only after EOF and verify that its completion marker and counts still match before applying. Keep the marker in unlogged storage with the staged rows so recovery clears both, and reload from the bound S3 version when the marker is missing. Use heartbeats for liveness and cancellation. Restart the stream for an incomplete generation in the first release. Record row errors durably with stable keys so retries do not duplicate errors. [PostgreSQL unlogged tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-createtable.html)
    28	
    29	### Inventory apply
    30	
    31	- Reuse the existing stable-frame lock, current-version uniqueness constraint, and close-and-append history. The repository already computes a boundary as the greater of database wall-clock time and the current valid_from plus one microsecond, then uses that boundary for the next version. Reuse this rule for all imported changes, including retirements. Preserve source_modified_at separately. The existing schema already stores versioned external references and links. Map each of the 45 CSV fields before adding new tables or moving attributes. Keep immutable history when normalizing shared site or spec data. [Schema](../frame-inventory-schema/frame-inventory-schema.md) [Repository](../../src/backend/src/main/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/frame/FrameRepository.java)
    32	- Define the content hash over canonical typed values, including versioned links and external references. Specify normalization, timezone and precision, null behavior, and duplicate-ID handling. Change manual UI/API writes to set source_modified_at from statement_timestamp() on the version insert after obtaining the frame lock. Preserve the source timestamp on CSV imports, including forced overwrites. Define how comparisons handle legacy manual versions that inherited an older source timestamp. A forced overwrite can move the current source timestamp backward. A separate source high-water mark remains an open decision.
    33	- Build one candidate per target key before set-based writes. Resolve shared dimensions and reserve frame identities before opening dependent versions and links. PostgreSQL 18 supports MERGE RETURNING, but a source candidate takes only one action, so close and append in separate set-based statements in the same transaction. Use the actual changed version IDs to produce outbox records. Commit versions, links, outbox, and final job status together. A retry after a lost commit response returns the committed result. [PostgreSQL MERGE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-merge.html)
    34	- Compute the retirement numerator and denominator on the same protected pre-apply inventory view. Row locks protect existing IDs, while new frames and edits that move into or out of scope require a shared writer protocol. Start with a transaction-scoped inventory lock held in shared mode by manual writes and DELTA applies, and in exclusive mode by snapshots. Take per-frame locks in stable ID order. This serializes promotion of snapshots even when their scopes are disjoint. Keep it out of upload, parsing, and staging. Measure lock time before enabling the feature. Never infer absence from a partial stream or an unrecoverable CSV parse error. Decide whether unidentifiable rows, scope violations, and header-only snapshots fail the whole job. The proposed default is to fail a snapshot before any inventory write when a safety check fails.
    35	
    36	### Snapshot watermark
    37	
    38	- Persist snapshot_as_of on the job. Accept a producer-supplied export watermark at job creation. When omitted, derive it from MAX(modified_date) after scanning the complete file. Use one documented source timezone and precision for comparisons. Require the exporter to supply an explicit watermark when the file cannot establish one. MAX(modified_date) measures the newest row change and can lag the time a complete export was generated. It also cannot prove completeness, so prefer the explicit export watermark for feeds where these times differ.
    39	- Use canonical scope keys in a containment hierarchy: GLOBAL, country, country/region, and country/region/environment. Require a region for every environment-level FULL_SNAPSHOT in the first release. Reject a country/environment scope such as UK/UNDERGROUND at job creation. An operator can export a separate authoritative snapshot for each region or use DELTA for a cross-region file.
    40	- Before inventory writes and under the snapshot apply lock, reject a watermark outside the freshness window (proposed default 24 hours), in the future beyond allowed clock skew, or strictly below the maximum committed watermark for the requested scope and its ancestors. Equal watermarks pass this check. On successful commit, advance only the requested scope's watermark, including when the job completes with row errors. A failed job leaves all watermarks as they were.
    41	- A newer descendant watermark does not reject an enclosing snapshot. Apply normal row conflict checks throughout the requested scope, including newer child scopes. Before retiring absent frames, exclude the entire subtree of each descendant whose committed watermark is strictly newer than the incoming watermark. Report the protected scopes and skipped retirement count. A descendant at the same watermark remains eligible. For example, a GLOBAL export at 11:30 can apply after a partition snapshot at 12:00, with retirement excluded in that partition. A partition export at 11:00 fails if an ancestor already committed at 12:00.
    42	- Among the remaining absent active frames, exclude any whose current valid_from or source_modified_at is after snapshot_as_of and record SKIPPED_RETIREMENT_NEWER_THAN_SNAPSHOT. This protects newer current versions, including edits within the same scope. Count only eligible retirements in the 10% numerator and keep the denominator as all pre-apply active frames in the declared scope. Capture the watermark checks, both exclusion counts, the breaker calculation, and the scope watermark update in the same protected apply transaction.
    43	
    44	### Snapshot history and reactivation
    45	
    46	The agreed representation is a new current version with status RETIRED and reason MISSING_FROM_FULL_SNAPSHOT. Define how current inventory queries treat that version and how a later import reactivates it. Existing manual deletion closes the last current version without opening a replacement. Keep those behaviors explicit in the status and history contract. If snapshot closure sets closed_by_change_source, extend the V2 constraint, which currently allows only MANUAL_DELETE. [V2 migration](../../src/backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__add_frame_change_source.sql)
    47	
    48	## Goals and non-goals
    49	
    50	- Deliver authenticated upload, visible job progress and row errors, retry-safe imports, audited versions, scoped retirement, and transactional outbox records.
    51	- Leave mass deletion, generalized CSV mapping, automatic repair of malformed source values, and multi-scope FULL_SNAPSHOT uploads outside the first release. If authoritative cross-region exports become a regular need, consider one atomic job over explicitly named scopes, each with its own watermark and retirement check.
    52	
    53	## Alternatives weighed
    54	
    55	- Keep the S3-to-Lambda bridge as requested. Direct S3-to-SQS delivery could remove an operational failure path if the bridge only forwards events. Verify what routing or event normalization the Lambda needs to own.
    56	- Keep UNLOGGED staging with full source replay for initial implementation. Durable staging could reduce replay cost and operational complexity after failover, at the cost of logging intermediate data. Benchmark with the expected maximum file.
    57	- Reuse versioned history as the initial design direction. Add a separate frame_history table only if it serves a distinct audited need. Otherwise two history stores would require agreement on which is authoritative.
    58	
    59	## Key decisions and implementation sequence
    60	
    61	1. Map the CSV to the current schema and the proposed six entities. Resolve source timestamp parsing, manual-edit ordering, force authorization, link semantics, duplicate IDs, and schema ownership before migrations.
    62	2. Add durable job, row error, lineage, and outbox storage through additive Flyway migrations. Expose BFF job creation and status, including counts, fatal errors, and paginated row errors. Set upload-size, row-count, timeout, and retention limits from the agreed operating envelope.
    63	3. Implement the S3 event bridge, SQS dispatch and DLQ, and Temporal start. Exercise duplicate notifications, late events, ambiguous starts, and reconciliation before applying inventory.
    64	4. Implement staging and atomic DELTA apply. Run the supplied CSV against PostgreSQL 18 and check replay, timestamp collisions, manual edits, forced overwrite, malformed quoting, duplicate IDs, lost staging, and worker failure immediately after commit.
    65	5. Add scoped FULL_SNAPSHOT with a protected retirement calculation. Verify that malformed rows with IDs stay present, out-of-scope frames stay untouched, and the exact 5% and 10% boundaries behave as agreed. Exercise rejection of environment scopes without a region, expired and out-of-order watermarks, watermark equality, derived watermarks, newer ancestors rejecting narrower snapshots, newer descendants protecting entire subtrees while present rows still upsert, frames created or moved into scope after export, and concurrent manual writes. Roll out DELTA first, then enable snapshot after observing apply times and reviewing operator safeguards.
    66	6. Track queue age and DLQ depth, time in each job state, staging retries, apply transaction duration, row error codes, retirement guard trips, and outbox lag. Correlate logs by job ID and keep presigned URLs and raw row content out of logs.
